simulation.Rmd

Simulation

amorem exposes a single front-door simulator, simulate_relational_events(), that composes five mechanisms on top of an event-by-event inner loop. Two algorithms drive the loop: Gillespie (exact, per-event) and τ-leap (approximate, fixed time slices). The two are compared at the bottom of this page. The examples on this page run when the page is built.

The five mechanisms

  1. Minimal Gillespie — homogeneous baseline rate over all admissible dyads.
  2. Per-dyad contribution logits — a static S × R matrix of log-rate adjustments (e.g. inter-state distances, role similarities).
  3. Exogenous sender / receiver covariates — per-actor numeric tables with their effect vectors.
  4. Endogenous statistics — any subset of the catalogue listed in Endogenous catalogue, updated after each fired event.
  5. Time-varying global covariates — piecewise-constant modifiers tied to an interval grid, advanced with a boundary-aware Gillespie scheme.

Per-feature argument map

Feature Arguments Notes
Dyad-level contribution contribution_logits S × R matrix of log-rate contributions
Static sender / receiver sender_covariates, sender_effects, receiver_covariates, receiver_effects per-actor tables; effects required
Endogenous endogenous_stats, endogenous_effects any stat from the catalogue
Exp-decay half-life half_life required when any *_exp_decay stat is active
Time-varying global global_covariates, global_effects piecewise constant on time_start intervals
Case–control output n_controls, wide ≥ 1 activates stratified output; wide = TRUE gives one row per event
Algorithm method, tau "gillespie" (exact) or "tau_leap"
Risk-set rule risk "standard" or "remove"

Idiomatic calls

Minimal Gillespie 

set.seed(1)
ev <- simulate_relational_events(
  n_events      = 500,
  senders       = LETTERS[1:6],
  receivers     = LETTERS[1:6],
  baseline_rate = 1)
head(ev)
#>   sender receiver       time
#> 1      A        C 0.02517273
#> 2      B        C 0.03002962
#> 3      D        E 0.09668795
#> 4      B        F 0.11122357
#> 5      C        F 0.17902660
#> 6      A        C 0.19149479

With a homogeneous rate every one of the 30 admissible dyads (no loops) is equally likely, so each dyad fires about 16.7 times on average; here the counts range from 9 to 26. Waiting times are exponential with rate 30 (baseline 1 per dyad), so the log spans 16.97 time units.

Per-dyad contribution logits

A static matrix shifts the log-rate of each dyad. Here dyads whose sender and receiver share a group get a log-rate bonus of 1.5:

actors <- paste0("a", 1:8)
group  <- rep(c("x", "y"), each = 4)
logits <- outer(group, group, function(a, b) ifelse(a == b, 1.5, 0))
dimnames(logits) <- list(actors, actors)
set.seed(2)
ev_g <- simulate_relational_events(
  n_events = 1000, senders = actors, receivers = actors,
  contribution_logits = logits)
within_share <- mean(group[match(ev_g$sender, actors)] ==
                     group[match(ev_g$receiver, actors)])
within_share
#> [1] 0.74

Within-group dyads make up 24 of the 56 admissible dyads; with weight exp(1.5) they should carry a share of 0.771 of the events, and the simulated share is 0.740.

Exogenous sender covariates

Per-actor covariates enter through a numeric table with one row per sender and a vector of effects:

actors <- paste0("a", 1:10)
set.seed(3)
activity <- data.frame(activity = seq(-1, 1, length.out = 10))
ev_x <- simulate_relational_events(
  n_events = 2000, senders = actors, receivers = actors,
  sender_covariates = activity, sender_effects = c(activity = 1))
sent <- as.vector(table(factor(ev_x$sender, levels = actors)))
cbind(activity, sent)
#>      activity sent
#> 1  -1.0000000   70
#> 2  -0.7777778   70
#> 3  -0.5555556   98
#> 4  -0.3333333  107
#> 5  -0.1111111  135
#> 6   0.1111111  196
#> 7   0.3333333  233
#> 8   0.5555556  278
#> 9   0.7777778  350
#> 10  1.0000000  463

The sender with the highest covariate value sends 463 events and the one with the lowest 70; their ratio, 6.61, compares with exp(2) = 7.39 implied by an effect of 1 over a covariate range of 2.

Endogenous structure 

set.seed(4)
ev_e <- simulate_relational_events(
  n_events           = 1000,
  senders            = letters[1:10],
  receivers          = letters[1:10],
  endogenous_stats   = c("reciprocity_count", "transitivity_count"),
  endogenous_effects = c(reciprocity_count  = 0.4,
                         transitivity_count = 0.3))
feats <- endogenous_features(ev_e, stats = c("reciprocity_count",
                                            "transitivity_count"))
summary(feats[, c("reciprocity_count", "transitivity_count")])
#>  reciprocity_count transitivity_count
#>  Min.   :  0.0     Min.   :0.000     
#>  1st Qu.: 41.0     1st Qu.:5.000     
#>  Median :165.5     Median :5.000     
#>  Mean   :172.9     Mean   :5.432     
#>  3rd Qu.:289.8     3rd Qu.:7.000     
#>  Max.   :414.0     Max.   :7.000

endogenous_features() recomputes the statistics from the timestamps alone; the simulator applies the same definitions while it generates the events (the Validation experiments, E5, compare the two row for row).

Case–control output

Set n_controls = k to emit a stratified case–control table directly: each fired event becomes one case row paired with k control rows drawn from the non-event risk set at that moment, sharing a stratum id.

set.seed(5)
cc <- simulate_relational_events(
  n_events           = 1200,
  senders            = paste0("a", 1:20),
  receivers          = paste0("a", 1:20),
  endogenous_stats   = "reciprocity_count",
  endogenous_effects = c(reciprocity_count = 0.6),
  n_controls         = 1)
head(cc[order(cc$stratum, -cc$event), ], 4)
#>   stratum event sender receiver        time reciprocity_count
#> 1       1     1     a2      a14 0.005231605                 0
#> 2       1     0    a15      a10 0.005231605                 0
#> 3       2     1     a1       a3 0.007413057                 0
#> 4       2     0    a17      a20 0.007413057                 0
library(survival)   # clogit() and strata()
fit <- clogit(event ~ reciprocity_count + strata(stratum), data = cc)
coef(fit)
#> reciprocity_count 
#>         0.4690212

The conditional-logit estimate from this one sample is 0.469 against the generating value 0.6. With wide = TRUE (and n_controls = 1) the same output comes as one row per event, ready for rem(method = "gam").

Time-varying global covariates 

g <- data.frame(time_start = c(0, 2, 5),
                weekend    = c(0, 1, 0))
set.seed(6)
ev_w <- simulate_relational_events(
  n_events          = 800,
  senders           = LETTERS[1:8],
  receivers         = LETTERS[1:8],
  baseline_rate     = 1,
  global_covariates = g,
  global_effects    = c(weekend = -1.5))
in_weekend <- ev_w$time >= 2 & ev_w$time < 5
rate_weekend <- sum(in_weekend) / 3
rate_week    <- sum(!in_weekend) / (max(ev_w$time) - 3)
c(events_per_unit_weekend = rate_weekend, events_per_unit_otherwise = rate_week)
#>   events_per_unit_weekend events_per_unit_otherwise 
#>                  16.00000                  56.92281

A boundary-aware Gillespie scheme advances the clock across each time_start boundary without recording or losing events. The event rate during the “weekend” interval [2, 5) is 16.0 per time unit against 56.9 outside it, a ratio of 0.281; the effect of −1.5 implies exp(-1.5) = 0.223. Each row also carries the covariate value at its time (weekend column).

Engines and the statistic catalogue

Both algorithms update the endogenous state from the realized events. The post-hoc endogenous_features() evaluates a statistic in compiled code when it is listed by cpp_supported_stats(), and in R otherwise:

supported <- cpp_supported_stats()
length(supported)
#> [1] 66
head(supported, 10)
#>  [1] "reciprocity"              "reciprocity_binary"      
#>  [3] "reciprocity_count"        "transitivity_binary"     
#>  [5] "transitivity_count"       "cyclic_binary"           
#>  [7] "cyclic_count"             "sending_balance_binary"  
#>  [9] "sending_balance_count"    "receiving_balance_binary"

Gillespie vs τ-leap

Same scenario in both algorithms: 50 actors, 2,000 events, a reciprocity_binary effect of 0.6, one control per case, 10 replicates per method. For each replicate we record the wall-clock of the simulator call and the conditional-logit estimate clogit(event ~ reciprocity_binary + strata(stratum)).

one_run <- function(seed, method, tau = NULL) {
  set.seed(seed)
  a <- paste0("a", 1:50)
  secs <- system.time(
    cc <- simulate_relational_events(
      n_events = 2000, senders = a, receivers = a, baseline_rate = 1,
      endogenous_stats = "reciprocity_binary",
      endogenous_effects = c(reciprocity_binary = 0.6),
      n_controls = 1, method = method, tau = tau)
  )[["elapsed"]]
  fit <- clogit(event ~ reciprocity_binary + strata(stratum),
                          data = cc)
  c(beta = coef(fit)[[1]], seconds = secs)
}
configs <- list(
  "Gillespie"      = list(method = "gillespie", tau = NULL),
  "tau-leap 0.01"  = list(method = "tau_leap",  tau = 0.01),
  "tau-leap 0.05"  = list(method = "tau_leap",  tau = 0.05),
  "tau-leap 0.20"  = list(method = "tau_leap",  tau = 0.20))
runs <- lapply(configs, function(cfg)
  t(vapply(1:10, one_run, numeric(2), method = cfg$method, tau = cfg$tau)))
tab <- t(vapply(runs, function(r) c(beta_mean = mean(r[, "beta"]),
                                    beta_sd   = stats::sd(r[, "beta"]),
                                    seconds   = mean(r[, "seconds"])),
                numeric(3)))
round(tab, 3)
#>               beta_mean beta_sd seconds
#> Gillespie         0.563   0.086   0.567
#> tau-leap 0.01     0.636   0.062   0.202
#> tau-leap 0.05     0.585   0.049   0.175
#> tau-leap 0.20     0.587   0.055   0.184
op <- par(mar = c(4, 4.5, 1, 1))
boxplot(lapply(runs, function(r) r[, "beta"]), ylab = expression(hat(beta)),
        col = "grey90")
abline(h = 0.6, lty = 2, col = "firebrick")

par(op)

The dashed line marks the generating value 0.6; at these settings the four distributions overlap. Across the ten replicates the mean estimate is 0.563 for Gillespie and 0.636, 0.585 and 0.587 for τ = 0.01, 0.05 and 0.20. With 50 actors the baseline alone produces about 2450 events per time unit, so a step of τ = 0.20 contains roughly 490 events that all share the start-of-step state; within a step, a dyad whose reverse fires earlier in the same step does not yet see it. Mean simulator time per run is 0.57 s for Gillespie and 0.17–0.20 s for τ-leap.

When to pick which

Use Gillespie when Use τ-leap when
Every event must react to every prior event Events within a step may share the start-of-step state
The model has effects that grow without bound (e.g. a large reciprocity_count effect), which τ-leap draws in large batches Wall-clock matters and τ has been checked against a small Gillespie run

When a single step would draw more than ten million events, simulate_relational_events() stops with a message instead. Choose τ so that the expected number of events per step is small relative to the size of the process, and check it against a Gillespie run of the same model; the Validation experiments report the wall-clock scaling with the number of actors.
